opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the text brain is where most of the intelligence actually lives right now. Over the past few years, almost all the gains in reasoning, in planning, in following complex instructions, came from scaling language models on text. Text is a very compressed form of human thinking. When people write things down, they've already done a lot of abstraction, so the model learns structure, logic and knowledge very efficiently from it.

Vision, audio and video are much higher bandwidth, but the signal is more diluted. A lot of pixels don't carry much information about reasoning. So if you train a multimodal model mostly from perception, it can become very good at recognizing things, but it doesn't necessarily become smarter. It might describe an image well but fail to reason about what it sees.

What we want is for the model to see something and then think about it with the same depth it has with text: solve the geometry problem in the picture, understand the chart and draw conclusions, debug the code from a screenshot. That requires the visual part to connect into the reasoning ability that was built on language, rather than being a separate system bolted on.

There's also a practical concern. When you add multimodal training, you often see the text ability degrade, a kind of "dumbing down." That's a bad trade. Ideally adding a new modality should be additive, or even mutually reinforcing, so the model gets broader perception without losing intelligence. Leaning on the text brain is how you keep that core intact.

So in the long run I see it as one unified model, with language as the backbone of thinking and the other modalities as new ways of taking in and acting on the world. Intelligence first, then extend its senses.

r001.rationale: The response says multimodal perception may not improve reasoning and that multimodal training can degrade text ability, but it does not mention mixture-of-experts models or warn against assigning experts exclusively to multimodality.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core reason is that intelligence, in the deepest sense, lives in language. When you look at what a language model learns from text, it's not just vocabulary or grammar. It's reasoning, abstraction, world knowledge, the ability to plan over long horizons. Text is the most compressed, most information-dense record of human thought that we have. People spent thousands of years distilling what they understand about the world into writing. So the text brain is where the real intelligence accumulates.

Now, if you train a vision model or a multimodal model from scratch, purely on images or video, you'll get something that perceives well, but it doesn't think well. It can recognize a cat, it can describe a scene, but ask it to reason about why something happened in the scene, or what should happen next, and it struggles. The reasoning capability just isn't there, because pixels don't carry that kind of structured, abstract signal in the same density.

So our view is that you shouldn't build a separate brain for each modality. You should have one brain, the one that already learned to think from text, and then teach it to see, to hear, to act. The visual signal becomes a new input channel into an existing reasoning engine, rather than a parallel system that has to rediscover reasoning on its own. That's also much more efficient. You're not wasting compute re-learning what the text model already knows.

There's a second reason, which is about scaling. Text data is finite, and we're approaching limits there. Multimodal data, especially video, is enormous. But raw video is mostly redundant, there's very little new information per frame. If you have a strong text brain, you can use it to extract the meaningful part from that data, to turn perception into something that actually adds to the model's understanding rather than just adding more parameters that memorize textures.

And ultimately, the goal isn't a model that's good at vision or good at language. It's a model that has a unified understanding of the world and can act in it. Language is the scaffolding for that understanding. Everything else should plug into it.

r001.rationale: The response argues for one shared reasoning brain instead of separate brains for each modality, but it does not mention mixture-of-experts models or warn that assigning experts exclusively to multimodality may weaken multimodal intelligence.

astra-6.text:
Because text contains a lot of knowledge and reasoning patterns that we want multimodal models to use. When a model sees an image or watches a video, we don’t want it to just recognize objects. We want it to connect what it sees to what it knows, understand the relationships, and reason about what might happen next.

So the idea of a “text brain” is to build on those capabilities instead of learning everything again for each modality. Vision and audio bring in information that text alone can’t capture, but they should be able to draw on the same underlying knowledge and reasoning. The challenge is making that connection while preserving the details that are unique to each modality.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sharing text knowledge and reasoning with other modalities, but does not warn that assigning experts exclusively to multimodality in a mixture-of-experts model may weaken multimodal intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
Because language already contains a lot of knowledge about the world. A model trained on text has learned concepts, relationships, and ways of reasoning. When we add vision or other modalities, we want the model to use those capabilities instead of learning everything again from scratch.

For example, recognizing an object in an image is one step. Understanding why it’s there, how it relates to other objects, or what might happen next requires knowledge and reasoning. Ideally, visual input can connect to the concepts the model already understands through language.

That doesn’t mean text can teach the model everything. Some things need to be learned directly from images, audio, or interaction. The goal is to bring that new information into a shared system, so the modalities can benefit from one another.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sharing language knowledge with other modalities, but it does not warn that assigning experts exclusively to multimodality in a mixture-of-experts model may produce weak multimodal intelligence.
